l: Christianity

Christianity is an <color=#3366CC>Abrahamic</color> <color=#3366CC>monotheistic</color> <color=#3366CC>religion</color> based on the <color=#3366CC>Bible</color> and the teachings of <color=#3366CC>Jesus</color>. The Gospels state
that Jesus is the Son of God and <color=#3366CC>rose from the dead</color> after <color=#3366CC>his crucifixion</color>, whose coming as the <color=#3366CC>messiah</color> (Christ) was
prophesied in the <color=#3366CC>Old Testament</color> and chronicled in the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color>. It is the world's largest and most widespread
religion with over 2.3 billion followers, comprising around 28.8% of the <color=#3366CC>world population</color>. Its adherents, known as
<color=#3366CC>Christians</color>, are estimated to make up a majority of the population in 120 countries and territories.
Christianity remains <color=#3366CC>culturally diverse</color> in its Western and <color=#3366CC>Eastern branches</color>, and doctrinally diverse concerning
<color=#3366CC>justification and the nature of salvation</color>, ecclesiology, ordination, and Christology. Most Christian denominations,
however, generally hold in common the belief that Jesus is <color=#3366CC>God the Son</color>—the Logos incarnated—who <color=#3366CC>ministered</color>,
suffered, and <color=#3366CC>died on a cross</color>, but <color=#3366CC>rose from the dead</color> for the salvation of humankind; this message is called <color=#3366CC>the gospel</color>,

meaning the "good news". The four canonical gospels of <color=#3366CC>Matthew</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mark</color>, <color=#3366CC>Luke</color> and <color=#3366CC>John</color> describe the <color=#3366CC>life of Jesus</color> and
teachings as preserved in the early Christian tradition, with the Old Testament as the gospels' respected background.
Christianity began in the 1st century, after the death of Jesus, as a Judaic sect with Hellenistic influence in the <color=#3366CC>Roman</color>
province of Judaea. The disciples of Jesus spread their faith around the Eastern Mediterranean area, despite
significant persecution. The inclusion of Gentiles led Christianity to slowly <color=#3366CC>separate from Judaism</color> in the 2nd century.
Emperor <color=#3366CC>Constantine I</color> decriminalized Christianity in the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> in 313 with the Edict of Milan. In 325,
Constantine convened the <color=#3366CC>Council of Nicaea</color>, where the <color=#3366CC>Nicene Creed</color> was adopted, and where Early Christianity was
consolidated into what would become the state religion by around 380. The <color=#3366CC>Church of the East</color> and <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodoxy</color>
both split over differences in Christology during the 5th century, while the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Church</color> separated in the <color=#3366CC>East–West Schism</color> in 1054. <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color> split into numerous denominations from the
Catholic Church during the <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color> era (16th century). Following the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> (15th–17th century),
Christianity expanded globally via <color=#3366CC>missionary work</color>, <color=#3366CC>evangelism</color>, immigration, and trade. Christianity played a prominent
role in the <color=#3366CC>development</color> of <color=#3366CC>Western civilization</color>, particularly in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> from late antiquity and the Middle Ages.

The three main <color=#3366CC>branches of Christianity</color> are <color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color> (1.3 billion people), <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color> (800 million), and <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>
<color=#3366CC>Orthodoxy</color> (300 million), while other prominent branches include <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodoxy</color> (60 million) and <color=#3366CC>Restorationism</color> (35
million). Smaller church communities number in the thousands. In Christianity, efforts toward unity (<color=#3366CC>ecumenism</color>) are
underway. In the <color=#3366CC>West</color>, Christianity remains the dominant religion even with a decline in adherence, with about 70% of
that population identifying as Christian. Christianity is growing in Africa and <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, the world's most populous continents.
Many Christians are still <color=#3366CC>persecuted</color> in some regions of the world, particularly where they are a minority, such as in the
<color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>, <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>.
Etymology
Early Jewish Christians referred to themselves as being of 'The Way', an expression possibly coming from Isaiah 40:3,
"prepare the way of the Lord". According to Acts 11:26, the term "Christian" (Khrīstiānós), meaning "followers of Christ"
and referring to Jesus' disciples, was first used in the city of Antioch by the non-Jewish inhabitants there. The earliest
recorded use of the term "Christianity/Christianism" (Khrīstiānismós) was by <color=#3366CC>Ignatius of Antioch</color> around 100 <color=#3366CC>AD</color>. The
name Jesus comes from (Iēsous), probably from.
History
Early Christianity
Apostolic Age
Christianity originated as a <color=#3366CC>Jewish movement</color> in Judaea during the 1st century AD, within the context of late Second
Temple Judaism. The earliest followers of Jesus were Jews who understood his life, death and expected return through
familiar Jewish apocalyptic and messianic frameworks. They remained embedded in <color=#3366CC>Jewish religious life</color> and did not
initially conceive of themselves as departing from Israel or founding a new faith. Following their conviction that Jesus
had been <color=#3366CC>raised from the dead</color>, they established a community in <color=#3366CC>Jerusalem</color> that awaited Jesus's <color=#3366CC>return</color> and
eschatological renewal, seeking to spread this message throughout Israel and the Jewish diaspora. Early Jewish
Christianity maintained a high Christology alongside monotheism. This early community was led by the three Pillars of
the Church, namely <color=#3366CC>James the Just</color>, <color=#3366CC>Peter</color>, and <color=#3366CC>John</color>. What eventually became of this earliest Christ-following
community remains unclear; they were possibly displaced, relocated, or killed when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem
in 70 AD.
Meanwhile, as the message about Jesus spread beyond <color=#3366CC>Judea</color> and <color=#3366CC>Galilee</color> into the broader Greco-Roman world, it
increasingly attracted Gentile adherents, especially among "God-fearers": non-Jews who were attracted to Judaism and
participated in <color=#3366CC>synagogal worship</color> without fully converting. This created a challenge for the movement's Jewish religious
outlook, which insisted on close observance of the Jewish commandments. Against this backdrop, <color=#3366CC>Paul the Apostle</color>, a
Jew of the <color=#3366CC>Pharisaic</color> school who had initially persecuted the Jesus movement, became one of its most influential
missionaries following his conversion, focusing on spreading the message to non-Jews in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Paul argued that Gentiles could participate in the promises of Israel through exclusive devotion to the God of Israel,
faith in Christ, <color=#3366CC>baptism</color>, and participation in his death and resurrection, without full adherence to the <color=#3366CC>Torah</color>, including
circumcision. This had a formative effect on the emerging <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> identity as <color=#3366CC>separate from Judaism</color>. Over time, such
developments contributed to the gradual differentiation between the Jesus movement and other Jewish communities, a
process that resulted in the emergence of Christianity as a separate religion.
Ante-Nicene period
This formative period was followed by the early <color=#3366CC>bishops</color>, whom Christians consider the successors of Christ's apostles.
From the year 150, Christian teachers began to produce theological and apologetic works aimed at defending the faith.
These authors are known as the Church Fathers, and the study of them is called patristics. Notable early Fathers

include <color=#3366CC>Ignatius of Antioch</color>, <color=#3366CC>Polycarp</color>, Justin Martyr, <color=#3366CC>Irenaeus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tertullian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Clement of Alexandria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Origen</color>.
During this period, there was no unified Christian movement but rather multiple competing sects, which held radically
different beliefs. Christian authors began using the Greek term hairesis, meaning "school of thought", to describe rival
communities, which gave rise to the concept of heresy. In the second and third centuries, figures like Justin Martyr,
<color=#3366CC>Irenaeus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tertullian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Clement of Alexandria</color>, often retrospectively referred to as "proto-orthodox", insisting that there
was one original apostolic teaching and that all rivals had deviated from it. Meanwhile, Valentinus, an <color=#3366CC>Alexandrian</color>
teacher, developed a <color=#3366CC>Gnostic</color> theology in which Christ brought saving knowledge (gnosis) that enabled believers to be
redeemed from the material world. <color=#3366CC>Marcion</color>, from Sinope, drew a distinction between high, purely good god, father of
Christ, and the lower, merely "just" god of Israel, who demanded sacrifice and procreation. Marcion is also known to
have assembled a collection of Christian texts, including his own gospel, and in doing so created one of the earliest
known Christian scriptural canons. Justin Martyr, from Neapolis, disagreed with both, arguing the God of the Jewish
scriptures was Christ himself before his incarnation. A gradual splitting off of Gentile Christianity left Jewish Christians
continuing to follow the Law of Moses, including practices such as circumcision. By the fifth century, they and the
Jewish–Christian gospels would be largely suppressed by the dominant sects in both Judaism and Christianity.
Christianity occupied an unstable position within the Roman world. In antiquity, what moderns call "religion" was closely
associated with ancestral traditions and embedded within other aspects of ethnic identity. It is possible that Gentile
Christians, having rejected their native gods, were perceived by their pagan neighbors as disrupting the relationship
between the divine and the community, on which civic welfare depended. Early examples of <color=#3366CC>persecution of Christians</color>
include the <color=#3366CC>Acts of the Apostles</color>, which portrays <color=#3366CC>Saint Stephen</color> as being killed by a mob in Jerusalem, while Paul writes
that he himself had persecuted Christians prior to his vision of Christ. Additionally, <color=#3366CC>Tacitus</color> wrote that Emperor <color=#3366CC>Nero</color>
blamed Christians for the <color=#3366CC>Great Fire of Rome</color> in 64 AD. In the following centuries, Church Fathers recorded
accusations that Christians were responsible for droughts, famines, and plagues. Nevertheless, before the mid-3rd
century, persecutions were often reactive, sporadic and local. This changed in 249, when the emperor Decius, who
ruled the empire following a long period of instability, ordered all residents of the empire (except Jews) to perform a
sacrifice to the <color=#3366CC>Roman gods</color>. Jews had long been excused on the basis of ancestral custom in ways that Christians,
lacking any such established tradition, were not. The Diocletianic Persecution beginning in 303 was particularly severe;
Christians were accused of attracting demons that disrupted traditional cult practices and threatened public order, and
were subjected to confiscations, destruction of buildings, expulsions, imprisonment, and demands for sacrifice. The
situation changed under <color=#3366CC>Constantine</color> (r. 306–337), who granted imperial support to Christianity, though under his rule
and that of his successors, forms deemed heretical were suppressed.
Spread in the Roman Empire
Christianity spread to <color=#3366CC>Aramaic</color>-speaking peoples along the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean coast</color> and also to the inland parts of the

<color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> and beyond that into the <color=#3366CC>Parthian Empire</color> and the later <color=#3366CC>Sasanian Empire</color>, including <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, which
was dominated at different times and to varying extents by these empires. The presence of Christianity in Africa began
in the middle of the 1st century in Egypt and by the end of the 2nd century in the region around <color=#3366CC>Carthage</color>. <color=#3366CC>Mark the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Evangelist</color> is claimed to have started the Church of Alexandria in about 43 AD; various later churches claim this as their
own legacy, including the <color=#3366CC>Coptic Orthodox Church</color>. Important Africans who influenced the early development of

Christianity include <color=#3366CC>Tertullian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Clement of Alexandria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Origen of Alexandria</color>, Cyprian, <color=#3366CC>Athanasius</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Augustine of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Hippo</color>.
<color=#3366CC>King Tiridates III</color> made Christianity the <color=#3366CC>state religion</color> in <color=#3366CC>Armenia</color> in the early 4th century, making Armenia the first
officially Christian state. It was not an entirely new religion in Armenia, having penetrated into the country from at least
the third century, but it may have been present even earlier.
<color=#3366CC>Constantine I</color> was exposed to Christianity in his youth, and throughout his life his support for the religion grew,
culminating in baptism on his deathbed. During his reign, state-sanctioned persecution of Christians was ended with
the Edict of Toleration in 311 and the Edict of Milan in 313. At that point, Christianity was still a minority belief,
comprising perhaps only 5% of the Roman population. Influenced by his adviser Mardonius, Constantine's nephew
Julian unsuccessfully tried to suppress Christianity. On 27 February 380, <color=#3366CC>Theodosius I</color>, Gratian, and Valentinian II
issued the Edict of Thessalonica establishing Nicene Christianity as the State church of the Roman Empire. As soon as
it became connected to the state, Christianity grew wealthy; the Church solicited donations from the rich and could now
own land.
Constantine was also instrumental in the convocation of the <color=#3366CC>First Council of Nicaea</color> in 325, which sought to address

<color=#3366CC>Arianism</color> and formulated the Nicene Creed, which is still used by in <color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodoxy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color>, and many other <color=#3366CC>Protestant</color> churches. Nicaea was the first of a series of <color=#3366CC>ecumenical councils</color>, which
formally defined critical elements of the theology of the Church, notably concerning Christology. The <color=#3366CC>Church of the East</color>
did not accept the third and following ecumenical councils and is still separate today by its successors (Assyrian
Church of the East).
In terms of prosperity and cultural life, the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> was one of the peaks in <color=#3366CC>Christian history</color> and Christian
civilization, and <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> remained the leading city of the <color=#3366CC>Christian world</color> in size, wealth, and culture. There was
a renewed interest in classical Greek philosophy, as well as an increase in literary output in vernacular Greek.
Byzantine art and literature held a preeminent place in Europe, and the cultural impact of <color=#3366CC>Byzantine art</color> on the West
during this period was enormous and of long-lasting significance. The later rise of <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> in North Africa reduced the size
and numbers of Christian congregations, leaving in large numbers only the <color=#3366CC>Coptic Church</color> in Egypt, the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Orthodox Tewahedo Church</color> in the Horn of Africa and the Nubian Church in the Sudan (Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia).
Middle Ages
Early Middle Ages
With the decline and <color=#3366CC>fall of the Roman Empire in the West</color>, the <color=#3366CC>papacy</color> became a political player, first visible in <color=#3366CC>Pope</color>
<color=#3366CC>Leo</color>'s diplomatic dealings with <color=#3366CC>Huns</color> and <color=#3366CC>Vandals</color>. The church also entered into a long period of missionary activity and
expansion among the various tribes. While <color=#3366CC>Arianists</color> instituted the death penalty for practicing pagans (see the
Massacre of Verden, for example), <color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color> also spread among the Hungarians, the <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Celtic</color>, the Baltic
and some <color=#3366CC>Slavic peoples</color>.
Around 500, Christianity was thoroughly integrated into Byzantine and <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Italy</color> culture and <color=#3366CC>Benedict of Nursia</color>
set out <color=#3366CC>his Monastic Rule</color>, establishing a system of regulations for the foundation and running of <color=#3366CC>monasteries</color>.
Monasticism became a powerful force throughout Europe, and gave rise to many early centers of learning, most
famously in <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color>, <color=#3366CC>Scotland</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Gaul</color>, contributing to the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color> of the 9th century.
In the 7th century, <color=#3366CC>Muslims conquered Syria</color> (including <color=#3366CC>Jerusalem</color>), North Africa, and Spain, converting some of the
Christian population to <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, including some of the Christian populations in pre-Islamic Arabia, and placing the rest
under a separate legal status. Part of the Muslims' success was due to the exhaustion of the Byzantine Empire in its
decades long conflict with <color=#3366CC>Persia</color>. Beginning in the 8th century, with the rise of <color=#3366CC>Carolingian</color> leaders, the Papacy sought
greater political support in the <color=#3366CC>Frankish Kingdom</color>.
The Middle Ages brought about major changes within the church. <color=#3366CC>Pope Gregory the Great</color> dramatically reformed the
ecclesiastical structure and administration. In the early 8th century, <color=#3366CC>iconoclasm</color> became a divisive issue, when it was
sponsored by the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> emperors. The Second Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (787) finally pronounced in favor of
icons. In the early 10th century, Western Christian monasticism was further rejuvenated through the leadership of the
great Benedictine monastery of <color=#3366CC>Cluny</color>.
High and Late Middle Ages
In the West, from the 11th century onward, some older cathedral schools became universities (see, for example,
<color=#3366CC>University of Oxford</color>, <color=#3366CC>University of Paris</color> and <color=#3366CC>University of Bologna</color>). Previously, higher education had been the domain
of Christian cathedral schools or monastic schools (Scholae monasticae), led by <color=#3366CC>monks</color> and <color=#3366CC>nuns</color>. Evidence of such
schools dates back to the 6th century AD. These new universities expanded the curriculum to include academic
programs for clerics, lawyers, civil servants, and physicians. The university is generally regarded as an institution that
has its origin in the <color=#3366CC>Medieval Christian</color> setting.
Accompanying the rise of the "new towns" throughout Europe, mendicant orders were founded, bringing the
consecrated religious life out of the monastery and into the new urban setting. The two principal mendicant movements

were the <color=#3366CC>Franciscans</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Dominicans</color>, founded by <color=#3366CC>Francis of Assisi</color> and <color=#3366CC>Dominic</color>, respectively. Both orders made
significant contributions to the development of the great universities of Europe. Another new order was the Cistercians,
whose large, isolated monasteries spearheaded the settlement of former wilderness areas. In this period, church
building and ecclesiastical architecture reached new heights, culminating in the orders of <color=#3366CC>Romanesque</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gothic</color>
<color=#3366CC>architecture</color> and the building of the great European cathedrals.
Christian nationalism emerged during this era in which Christians felt the desire to recover lands in which Christianity
had historically flourished. From 1095 under the pontificate of <color=#3366CC>Urban II</color>, the <color=#3366CC>First Crusade</color> was launched. These were a
series of military campaigns in the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color> and elsewhere, initiated in response to pleas from the Byzantine Emperor
<color=#3366CC>Alexios I</color> for aid against Turkish expansion. The Crusades ultimately failed to stifle Islamic aggression and even
contributed to Christian enmity with the sacking of <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Fourth Crusade</color>.
The Christian Church experienced internal conflict between the 7th and 13th centuries that resulted in a <color=#3366CC>schism</color>
between the Latin Church of Western Christianity branch, the now-Catholic Church, and an <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>, largely Greek,
branch (the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color>). The two sides disagreed on a number of administrative, liturgical and doctrinal
issues, most prominently Eastern Orthodox opposition to papal supremacy. The Second Council of Lyon (1274) and
the Council of Florence (1439) attempted to reunite the churches, but in both cases, the Eastern Orthodox refused to
implement the decisions, and the two principal churches remain in schism to the present day. However, the Catholic
Church has achieved union with various <color=#3366CC>smaller eastern churches</color>.
In the thirteenth century, a new emphasis on Jesus' suffering, exemplified by the Franciscans' preaching, had the
consequence of turning worshippers' attention towards Jews, on whom Christians had placed the blame for Jesus'
death. Christianity's limited tolerance of Jews was not new—Augustine of Hippo said that Jews should not be allowed
to enjoy the citizenship that Christians took for granted—but the growing antipathy towards Jews was a factor that led
to the expulsion of Jews from England in 1290, the first of many such expulsions in Europe.
Beginning around 1184, following the crusade against <color=#3366CC>Cathar</color> heresy, various institutions, broadly referred to as the
<color=#3366CC>Inquisition</color>, were established with the aim of suppressing <color=#3366CC>heresy</color> and securing religious and doctrinal unity within
Christianity through <color=#3366CC>conversion</color> and prosecution.
Modern era
Reformation and response
The 15th-century <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> brought about a renewed interest in ancient and classical learning. During the

<color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color> posted the <color=#3366CC>Ninety-five Theses</color> 1517 against the sale of <color=#3366CC>indulgences</color>. Printed copies soon
spread throughout Europe. In 1521 the Edict of Worms condemned and excommunicated Luther and his followers,
resulting in the schism of the Western Christendom into several branches.

Other reformers like <color=#3366CC>Zwingli</color>, Oecolampadius, <color=#3366CC>Calvin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Knox</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Arminius</color> further criticized Catholic teaching and
worship. These challenges developed into the movement called <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color>, which repudiated the primacy of the
pope, the role of tradition, the seven sacraments, and other doctrines and practices. The <color=#3366CC>Reformation in England</color> began
in 1534, when King <color=#3366CC>Henry VIII</color> had himself declared head of the <color=#3366CC>Church of England</color>. Beginning in 1536, the monasteries
throughout England, Wales and Ireland were dissolved.
<color=#3366CC>Thomas Müntzer</color>, Andreas Karlstadt and other theologians perceived both the Catholic Church and the confessions of
the Magisterial Reformation as corrupted. Their activity brought about the Radical Reformation, which gave birth to
various <color=#3366CC>Anabaptist</color> denominations.
Partly in response to the Protestant Reformation, the Catholic Church engaged in a substantial process of reform and
renewal, known as the <color=#3366CC>Counter-Reformation</color> or Catholic Reform. The <color=#3366CC>Council of Trent</color> clarified and reasserted Catholic
doctrine. During the following centuries, competition between Catholicism and Protestantism became deeply entangled
with political struggles among European states.
Meanwhile, the discovery of America by <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> in 1492 brought about a new wave of missionary
activity. Partly from missionary zeal, but under the impetus of <color=#3366CC>colonial expansion</color> by the European powers, Christianity
spread to the Americas, Oceania, East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
Throughout Europe, the division caused by the Reformation led to outbreaks of <color=#3366CC>religious violence</color> and the
establishment of separate state churches in Europe. <color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color> spread into the northern, central, and eastern parts of
present-day Germany, <color=#3366CC>Livonia</color>, and Scandinavia. <color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color> was established in England in 1534. <color=#3366CC>Calvinism</color> and its
varieties, such as <color=#3366CC>Presbyterianism</color>, were introduced in Scotland, the Netherlands, Hungary, Switzerland, and France.
<color=#3366CC>Arminianism</color> gained followers in the Netherlands and <color=#3366CC>Frisia</color>. Ultimately, these differences led to the outbreak of <color=#3366CC>conflicts</color>
in which religion played a key factor. The <color=#3366CC>Thirty Years' War</color>, the <color=#3366CC>English Civil War</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>French Wars of Religion</color> are
prominent examples. These events intensified the Christian debate on persecution and toleration.
In the revival of neoplatonism Renaissance humanists did not reject Christianity; quite the contrary, many of the
greatest works of the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> were devoted to it, and the Catholic Church patronized many works of <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>
<color=#3366CC>art</color>. Much, if not most, of the new art was commissioned by or in dedication to the Church. Some scholars and
historians attribute Christianity to having contributed to the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color>. Many well-known historical
figures who influenced <color=#3366CC>Western science</color> considered themselves Christian such as <color=#3366CC>Nicolaus Copernicus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Galileo Galilei</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Johannes Kepler</color>, <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color> and <color=#3366CC>Robert Boyle</color>.
Post-Enlightenment
In the era known as the <color=#3366CC>Great Divergence</color>, when in the West, the <color=#3366CC>Age of Enlightenment</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color>
brought about great societal changes, Christianity was confronted with various forms of <color=#3366CC>skepticism</color> and with certain

modern <color=#3366CC>political ideologies</color>, such as versions of <color=#3366CC>socialism</color> and <color=#3366CC>liberalism</color>. Events ranged from mere <color=#3366CC>anti-clericalism</color> to
violent outbursts against Christianity, such as the dechristianization of France during the French Revolution, the
<color=#3366CC>Spanish Civil War</color>, and certain <color=#3366CC>Marxist</color> movements, especially <color=#3366CC>the Russian Revolution</color> and the persecution of Christians
in the Soviet Union under state atheism.
Especially pressing in Europe was the formation of <color=#3366CC>nation states</color> after the Napoleonic era. In all European countries,
different Christian denominations found themselves in competition to greater or lesser extents with each other and with
the state. Variables were the relative sizes of the denominations and the religious, political, and ideological orientation
of the states. Urs Altermatt of the University of Fribourg, looking specifically at Catholicism in Europe, identifies four
models for the European nations. In traditionally Catholic-majority countries such as Belgium, Spain, and Austria, to
some extent, religious and national communities are more or less identical. Cultural symbiosis and separation are
found in Poland, the Republic of Ireland, and Switzerland, all countries with competing denominations. Competition is
found in Germany, the Netherlands, and again Switzerland, all countries with minority Catholic populations, which to a
greater or lesser extent identified with the nation. Finally, separation between religion (again, specifically Catholicism)
and the state is found to a great degree in France and Italy, countries where the state actively opposed itself to the
authority of the Catholic Church.
The combined factors of the formation of nation states and ultramontanism, especially in Germany and the
Netherlands, but also in England to a much lesser extent, often forced Catholic churches, organizations, and believers
to choose between the national demands of the state and the authority of the Church, specifically the papacy. This
conflict came to a head in the First Vatican Council, and in Germany would lead directly to the Kulturkampf.
Christian commitment in Europe dropped as modernity and secularism came into their own, particularly in the <color=#3366CC>Czech</color>
<color=#3366CC>Republic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Estonia</color>, while religious commitments in America have been generally high in comparison to Europe.
Changes in worldwide Christianity over the last century have been significant, since 1900, Christianity has spread
rapidly in the <color=#3366CC>Global South</color> and Third World countries. The late 20th century has shown the shift of Christian adherence
to the <color=#3366CC>Third World</color> and the Southern Hemisphere in general, with the West no longer the chief standard bearer of
Christianity. Approximately 7 to 10% of <color=#3366CC>Arabs</color> are Christians, most prevalent in Egypt, <color=#3366CC>Syria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>.
Beliefs
While Christians worldwide share basic convictions, there are differences of interpretations and opinions of the <color=#3366CC>Bible</color>
and <color=#3366CC>sacred traditions</color> on which Christianity is based. Christianity encompasses various movements of <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>
<color=#3366CC>theology</color>, the main ones being conservative <color=#3366CC>fundamentalist</color> or moderate, liberal and progressive.
Creeds
Concise doctrinal statements or confessions of religious beliefs are known as <color=#3366CC>creeds</color>. They began as baptismal
formulae and were later expanded during the Christological controversies of the 4th and 5th centuries to become
statements of faith. "Jesus is Lord" is the earliest creed of Christianity and continues to be used, as with the <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>Council of Churches</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Apostles' Creed</color> is the most widely accepted statement of the articles of Christian faith. It is used by a number of
Christian denominations for both <color=#3366CC>liturgical</color> and catechetical purposes, most visibly by liturgical churches of Western
Christian tradition, including the Latin Church of the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color>, and Western Rite
Orthodoxy. It is also used by <color=#3366CC>Presbyterians</color>, <color=#3366CC>Methodists</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Congregationalists</color>.
This particular creed was developed between the 2nd and 9th centuries. Its central doctrines are those of the <color=#3366CC>Trinity</color>
and God the <color=#3366CC>Creator</color>. Each of the doctrines found in this creed can be traced to statements current in the apostolic
period. The creed was apparently used as a summary of Christian doctrine for baptismal candidates in the churches of
Rome. Its points include:
• Belief in <color=#3366CC>God the Father</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jesus Christ</color> as the <color=#3366CC>Son of God</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Holy Spirit</color>
• The <color=#3366CC>death</color>, descent into hell, <color=#3366CC>resurrection</color> and ascension of Christ
• The holiness of the Church and the communion of saints
• Christ's <color=#3366CC>second coming</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Day of Judgement</color> and salvation of the faithful
The <color=#3366CC>Nicene Creed</color> was formulated, largely in response to <color=#3366CC>Arianism</color>, at the Councils of <color=#3366CC>Nicaea</color> and Constantinople in
325 and 381 respectively, and ratified as the universal creed of <color=#3366CC>Christendom</color> by the First Council of Ephesus in 431.
The Chalcedonian Definition, or Creed of Chalcedon, developed at the <color=#3366CC>Council of Chalcedon</color> in 451, though rejected by
the <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox</color>, taught Christ "to be acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly,
inseparably": one divine and one human, and that both natures, while perfect in themselves, are nevertheless also
perfectly united into one person.
The Athanasian Creed, received in the Western Church as having the same status as the Nicene and Chalcedonian,
says: "We worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confounding the Persons nor dividing the Substance".

Most Christians (<color=#3366CC>Catholic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Protestant</color> alike) accept the use of creeds and
subscribe to at least one of the creeds mentioned above.
Certain <color=#3366CC>Evangelical Protestants</color>, though not all of them, reject creeds as definitive statements of faith, even while
agreeing with some or all of the substance of the creeds. Also rejecting creeds are groups with roots in the Restoration
Movement, such as the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), the Evangelical Christian Church in Canada, and the
Churches of Christ.
Jesus
The central tenet of Christianity is the belief in <color=#3366CC>Jesus</color> as the Son of God and the <color=#3366CC>Messiah</color> (Christ). Christians believe
that Jesus, as the Messiah, was anointed by God as savior of humanity and hold that Jesus' coming was the fulfillment
of messianic prophecies of the <color=#3366CC>Old Testament</color>. The Christian concept of messiah differs significantly from the
contemporary Jewish concept. The core Christian belief is that through belief in and acceptance of <color=#3366CC>the death and</color>
<color=#3366CC>resurrection of Jesus</color>, <color=#3366CC>sinful</color> humans can be reconciled to God, and thereby are offered salvation and the promise of
<color=#3366CC>eternal life</color>.
While there have been many <color=#3366CC>theological</color> disputes over the nature of Jesus over the earliest centuries of Christian
history, generally, Christians believe that Jesus is God incarnate and "true God and true man" (or both fully divine and
fully human). Jesus, having become fully human, suffered the pains and temptations of a mortal man, but did not sin.
As fully God, he rose to life again. According to the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color>, he <color=#3366CC>rose</color> from the dead, ascended to heaven, is
seated at the right hand of the Father, and will ultimately <color=#3366CC>return</color> to fulfill the rest of the Messianic prophecy, including the
resurrection of the dead, the <color=#3366CC>Last Judgment</color>, and the final establishment of the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of God</color>.

According to the canonical gospels of <color=#3366CC>Matthew</color> and <color=#3366CC>Luke</color>, Jesus was conceived by the <color=#3366CC>Holy Spirit</color> and <color=#3366CC>born</color> from <color=#3366CC>the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Virgin Mary</color>. Little of Jesus' childhood is recorded in the canonical gospels, although infancy gospels were popular in
antiquity. In comparison, his adulthood, especially the week before his death, is well documented in the gospels
contained within the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color>, because that part of his life is believed to be most important. The biblical
accounts of <color=#3366CC>Jesus' ministry</color> include: his baptism, miracles, preaching, teaching, and deeds.
Death and resurrection
Christians consider the resurrection of Jesus to be the cornerstone of their faith (see 1 Corinthians 15). Among
Christian beliefs, the death and resurrection of Jesus are two core events on which much of Christian doctrine and
theology is based. According to the New Testament, Jesus was <color=#3366CC>crucified</color>, died a physical death, was buried within a
tomb, and rose from the dead three days later.
The New Testament mentions several <color=#3366CC>post-resurrection appearances of Jesus</color> on different occasions to his <color=#3366CC>twelve</color>
<color=#3366CC>apostles</color> and disciples, including "more than five hundred brethren at once", before Jesus' ascension to heaven. Jesus'
death and resurrection are commemorated by Christians in all worship services, with special emphasis during Holy
Week, which includes <color=#3366CC>Good Friday</color> and <color=#3366CC>Easter</color> Sunday.
The death and resurrection of Jesus are usually considered the most important events in <color=#3366CC>Christian theology</color>, partly
because they demonstrate that Jesus has power over life and death and therefore has the authority and power to give
people eternal life.
Christian churches accept and teach the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color> account of the resurrection of Jesus with very few exceptions.
Some modern scholars use the belief of Jesus' followers in the resurrection as a point of departure for establishing the
continuity of the historical Jesus and the proclamation of the early church. Some liberal Christians do not accept a
literal bodily resurrection, seeing the story as richly symbolic and spiritually nourishing <color=#3366CC>myth</color>. Arguments over death and
resurrection claims occur at many religious <color=#3366CC>debates</color> and interfaith dialogues. <color=#3366CC>Paul the Apostle</color>, an early Christian
convert and missionary, wrote, "If Christ was not raised, then all our preaching is useless, and your trust in God is
useless".
Salvation
"For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have
eternal life".
<color=#3366CC>Paul the Apostle</color>, like Jews and Roman <color=#3366CC>pagans</color> of his time, believed that sacrifice can bring about new kinship ties,
purity, and eternal life. For Paul, the necessary sacrifice was the death of Jesus: Gentiles who are "Christ's" are, like
Israel, descendants of Abraham and "heirs according to the promise" The God who raised Jesus from the dead would
also give new life to the "mortal bodies" of Gentile Christians, who had become with Israel, the "children of God", and
were therefore no longer "in the flesh".
Modern Christian churches tend to be much more concerned with how humanity can be <color=#3366CC>saved</color> from a universal
condition of sin and death than the question of how both Jews and Gentiles can be in God's family. According to
<color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color> theology, based upon their understanding of the atonement as put forward by Irenaeus' <color=#3366CC>recapitulation</color>
<color=#3366CC>theory</color>, Jesus' death is a ransom. This restores the relation with God, who is loving and reaches out to humanity, and
offers the possibility of theosis c.q. divinization, becoming the kind of humans God wants humanity to be. The Catholic
church also holds to a form of ransom theory but also teaches that Jesus' death satisfies the debt to the Father incurred
by the sins of humanity. The Catholic Church further affirms that salvation does not occur without faithfulness on the
part of Christians; converts must live in accordance with principles of love and ordinarily must be baptized. In Protestant
theology, Jesus' death is regarded as a substitutionary penalty carried by Jesus, for the debt that has to be paid by
humankind when it broke God's moral law.
Christians differ in their views on the extent to which individuals' salvation is pre-ordained by God. Reformed theology
places distinctive emphasis on grace by teaching that individuals are completely incapable of self-redemption, but that
sanctifying grace is irresistible. In contrast <color=#3366CC>Catholics</color>, Orthodox Christians, and <color=#3366CC>Arminian</color> Protestants believe that the
exercise of <color=#3366CC>free will</color> is necessary to have faith in Jesus.
Trinity
Trinity refers to the teaching that the one God comprises three distinct, eternally co-existing persons: the <color=#3366CC>Father</color>, the
Son (incarnate in Jesus Christ) and the <color=#3366CC>Holy Spirit</color>. Together, these three persons are sometimes called the Godhead,
although there is no single term in use in Scripture to denote the unified Godhead. In the words of the Athanasian
Creed, an early statement of Christian belief, "the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and yet
there are not three Gods but one God". They are distinct from another: the Father has no source, the Son is begotten of
the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Though distinct, the three persons cannot be divided from one
another in being or in operation. While some Christians also believe that God appeared as the Father in the <color=#3366CC>Old</color>
<color=#3366CC>Testament</color>, it is agreed that he appeared as the Son in the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color> and will still continue to manifest as the
Holy Spirit in the present. But still, God still existed as three persons in each of these times. However, traditionally there
is a belief that it was the Son who appeared in the Old Testament because, for example, when the <color=#3366CC>Trinity is depicted in</color>
<color=#3366CC>art</color>, the Son typically has the distinctive appearance, a cruciform halo identifying Christ, and in depictions of the <color=#3366CC>Garden</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Eden</color>, this looks forward to an Incarnation yet to occur. In some Early Christian <color=#3366CC>sarcophagi</color>, the Logos is
distinguished with a beard, "which allows him to appear ancient, even pre-existent".
The <color=#3366CC>Trinity</color> is an essential doctrine of mainstream Christianity. From earlier than the times of the Nicene Creed (325)
Christianity advocated the triune mystery-nature of God as a normative profession of faith. According to Roger E. Olson
and Christopher Hall, through prayer, meditation, study and practice, the Christian community concluded "that God
must exist as both a unity and trinity", codifying this in ecumenical council at the end of the 4th century.
According to this doctrine, God is not divided in the sense that each person has a third of the whole; rather, each
person is considered to be fully God (see Perichoresis). The distinction lies in their relations, the Father being
unbegotten; the Son being begotten of the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and (in Western
Christian theology) from the Son. Regardless of this apparent difference, the three "persons" are each <color=#3366CC>eternal</color> and
omnipotent. Other Christian religions including <color=#3366CC>Unitarian Universalism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jehovah's Witnesses</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Mormonism</color>, do not
share those views on the Trinity.
The Greek word trias is first seen in this sense in the works of Theophilus of Antioch; his text reads: "of the Trinity, of
God, and of His Word, and of His Wisdom". The term may have been in use before this time; its Latin equivalent,
trinitas, appears afterwards with an explicit reference to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in <color=#3366CC>Tertullian</color>. In the
following century, the word was in general use. It is found in many passages of <color=#3366CC>Origen</color>.
Trinitarianism
Trinitarianism denotes Christians who believe in the concept of the <color=#3366CC>Trinity</color>. Almost all Christian denominations and
churches hold Trinitarian beliefs. Although the words "Trinity" and "Triune" do not appear in the Bible, beginning in the
3rd century theologians developed the term and concept to facilitate apprehension of the New Testament teachings of
God as being Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since that time, Christian theologians have been careful to emphasize that
Trinity does not imply that there are three gods (the antitrinitarian heresy of Tritheism), nor that each hypostasis of the
Trinity is one-third of an infinite God (partialism), nor that the Son and the Holy Spirit are beings created by and
subordinate to the Father (<color=#3366CC>Arianism</color>). Rather, the Trinity is defined as one God in three persons.
Nontrinitarianism
Nontrinitarianism (or antitrinitarianism) refers to theology that rejects the doctrine of the Trinity. Various nontrinitarian
views, such as adoptionism or modalism, existed in early Christianity, leading to disputes about Christology.
Nontrinitarianism reappeared in the <color=#3366CC>Gnosticism</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Cathars</color> between the 11th and 13th centuries, among groups
with <color=#3366CC>Unitarian</color> theology in the <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color> of the 16th century, in the 18th-century <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color>, among
<color=#3366CC>Restorationist</color> groups arising during the <color=#3366CC>Second Great Awakening</color> of the 19th century, and most recently, in Oneness
Pentecostal churches.
Eschatology
The end of things, whether the end of an individual life, the end of the age, or the end of the world, broadly speaking, is
Christian eschatology; the study of the destiny of humans as it is revealed in the Bible. The major issues in Christian
eschatology are the <color=#3366CC>Tribulation</color>, death and the afterlife, (mainly for <color=#3366CC>Evangelical</color> groups) <color=#3366CC>the Millennium</color> and the following

<color=#3366CC>Rapture</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Second Coming</color> of Jesus, Resurrection of the Dead, Heaven, (for <color=#3366CC>liturgical</color> branches) <color=#3366CC>Purgatory</color>, and Hell,
the <color=#3366CC>Last Judgment</color>, the end of the world, and the <color=#3366CC>New Heavens and New Earth</color>.
Christians believe that the second coming of Christ will occur at the <color=#3366CC>end of time</color>, after a period of severe persecution
(the Great Tribulation). All who have died will be resurrected bodily from the dead for the Last Judgment. Jesus will fully
establish the Kingdom of God in fulfillment of scriptural prophecies.
Death and afterlife
Most Christians believe that human beings experience divine judgment and are rewarded either with eternal life or
<color=#3366CC>eternal damnation</color>. This includes the <color=#3366CC>general judgement</color> at the resurrection of the dead as well as the belief (held by
Catholics, Orthodox and most Protestants) in a judgment particular to the individual soul after physical death.
In the Catholic branch of Christianity, those who die in a state of grace, i.e., without any mortal sin separating them
from God, but are still imperfectly purified from the effects of sin, undergo purification through the intermediate state of
<color=#3366CC>purgatory</color> to achieve the holiness necessary for entrance into God's presence. Those who have attained this goal are
called saints (Latin sanctus, "holy").
Some Christian groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists, hold to mortalism, the belief that the human soul is not
naturally immortal, and is unconscious during the intermediate state between bodily death and resurrection. These
Christians also hold to Annihilationism, the belief that subsequent to the final judgement, the wicked will cease to exist
rather than suffer everlasting torment. Jehovah's Witnesses hold to a similar view.
Practices
Depending on the specific <color=#3366CC>denomination of Christianity</color>, practices may include <color=#3366CC>baptism</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Eucharist</color> (Holy Communion

or the Lord's Supper), <color=#3366CC>prayer</color> (including the <color=#3366CC>Lord's Prayer</color>), <color=#3366CC>confession</color>, <color=#3366CC>confirmation</color>, burial rites, marriage rites and the
religious education of children. Most denominations have ordained <color=#3366CC>clergy</color> who lead regular worship services.
Christian rites, rituals, and ceremonies are not celebrated in one single sacred language. Many ritualistic Christian
churches make a distinction between sacred language, liturgical language and vernacular language. The three
important languages in the early Christian era were: <color=#3366CC>Latin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> and <color=#3366CC>Syriac</color>.
Communal worship
<color=#3366CC>Services</color> of worship typically follow a pattern or form known as <color=#3366CC>liturgy</color>. Justin Martyr described 2nd-century Christian
liturgy in his First Apology (c. 150) to Emperor <color=#3366CC>Antoninus Pius</color>, and his description remains relevant to the basic
structure of Christian liturgical worship:
And Sundays, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or
the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally
instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and pray, and, as we before said,
when our prayer is ended, bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and
thanksgivings, according to his ability, and the people assent, saying <color=#3366CC>Amen</color>; and there is a distribution to each, and a
participation of that over which thanks have been given, and to those who are absent a portion is sent by the deacons.
And they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit; and what is collected is deposited with the president,
who succours the orphans and widows and those who, through sickness or any other cause, are in want, and those
who are in bonds and the strangers sojourning among us, and in a word takes care of all who are in need.
Thus, as Justin described, Christians assemble for communal worship typically on Sunday, the Lord's Day, though
other liturgical practices often occur outside this setting. Scripture readings are drawn from the Old and New
Testaments, but especially the gospels. Instruction is given based on these readings, in the form of a <color=#3366CC>sermon</color> or homily.
There are a variety of <color=#3366CC>congregational</color> prayers, including thanksgiving, confession, and intercession, which occur
throughout the service and take a variety of forms including recited, responsive, silent, or sung. <color=#3366CC>Psalms</color>, <color=#3366CC>hymns</color>,
worship songs, and other <color=#3366CC>church music</color> may be sung. Services can be varied for special events like significant feast
days.
Nearly all forms of worship incorporate the Eucharist, which consists of bread and wine (or a substitute). It is reenacted
in accordance with Jesus' instruction at the <color=#3366CC>Last Supper</color> that his followers do in remembrance of him as when he gave
his disciples bread, saying, "This is my body", and gave them wine saying, "This is my blood". In the early church,
Christians and those yet to complete initiation would separate for the Eucharistic part of the service. Some
denominations such as Confessional Lutheran churches continue to practice 'closed communion'. They offer
communion to those who are already united in that denomination or sometimes individual church. Catholics further
restrict participation to their members who are not in a state of <color=#3366CC>mortal sin</color>. Many other churches, such as the Anglican
Communion and the <color=#3366CC>Methodist Churches</color> (such as the Free Methodist Church and <color=#3366CC>United Methodist Church</color>), practice
'open communion' since they view communion as a means to unity, rather than an end, and invite all believing
Christians to participate.
Sacraments or ordinances
And this food is called among us Eukharistia [the Eucharist], of which no one is allowed to partake but the man who
believes that the things which we teach are true, and who has been washed with the washing that is for the remission
of sins, and unto regeneration, and who is so living as Christ has enjoined. For not as common bread and common
drink do we receive these; but in like manner as Jesus Christ our Savior, having been made flesh by the Word of God,
had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so likewise have we been taught that the food which is blessed by the prayer
of His word, and from which our blood and flesh by transmutation are nourished, is the flesh and blood of that Jesus
who was made flesh.
In Christian belief and practice, a sacrament is a <color=#3366CC>rite</color>, instituted by Christ, that confers grace, constituting a sacred
mystery. The term is derived from the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> word sacramentum, which was used to translate the Greek word for
mystery. Views concerning both which rites are sacramental, and what it means for an act to be a sacrament, vary
among Christian denominations and traditions.
The most conventional functional definition of a sacrament is that it is an outward sign, instituted by Christ, that conveys
an inward, spiritual grace through Christ. The two most widely accepted sacraments are <color=#3366CC>Baptism</color> and the Eucharist;
however, the majority of Christians also recognize five additional sacraments: <color=#3366CC>Confirmation</color> (Chrismation in the Eastern

tradition), <color=#3366CC>Holy Orders</color> (or ordination), <color=#3366CC>Penance</color> (or <color=#3366CC>Confession</color>), <color=#3366CC>Anointing of the Sick</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Matrimony</color> (see Christian
views on marriage).
Taken together, these are the Seven Sacraments as recognized by churches in the High Church tradition—notably

Catholic, <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox</color>, Independent Catholic, <color=#3366CC>Old Catholic</color>, some <color=#3366CC>Lutherans</color> and Anglicans.
Most other denominations and traditions typically affirm only Baptism and Eucharist as sacraments, while some
Protestant groups, such as the Quakers, reject sacramental theology. Certain denominations of Christianity, such as
Anabaptists, use the term "ordinances" to refer to rites instituted by Jesus for Christians to observe. Seven ordinances
have been taught in many Conservative Mennonite Anabaptist churches, which include "baptism, communion,
footwashing, marriage, anointing with oil, the holy kiss, and the prayer covering".
In addition to this, the <color=#3366CC>Church of the East</color> has two additional sacraments in place of the traditional sacraments of
Matrimony and the Anointing of the Sick. These include Holy Leaven (Melka) and the sign of the cross. The
<color=#3366CC>Schwarzenau Brethren</color> Anabaptist churches, such as the Dunkard Brethren Church, observe the agape feast
(lovefeast), a rite also observed by <color=#3366CC>Moravian Church</color> and <color=#3366CC>Methodist Churches</color>.
Liturgical calendar
Catholics, Eastern Christians, Lutherans, Anglicans and other traditional Protestant communities frame worship around
the <color=#3366CC>liturgical year</color>. The liturgical cycle divides the year into a series of <color=#3366CC>seasons</color>, each with their theological emphases,
and modes of prayer, which can be signified by different ways of decorating churches, colors of paraments and
vestments for clergy, scriptural readings, themes for preaching and even different traditions and practices often
observed personally or in the home.
Western Christian liturgical calendars are based on the cycle of the Roman Rite of the Catholic Church, and Eastern
Christians use analogous calendars based on the cycle of their respective rites. Calendars set aside holy days, such as
solemnities which commemorate an event in the life of Jesus, Mary, or the <color=#3366CC>saints</color>, and periods of <color=#3366CC>fasting</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>Lent</color>
and other pious events such as memoria, or lesser festivals commemorating saints. Christian groups that do not follow
a liturgical tradition often retain certain celebrations, such as <color=#3366CC>Christmas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Easter</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Pentecost</color>: these are the
celebrations of Christ's birth, resurrection, and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Church, respectively. A few
denominations such as <color=#3366CC>Quaker Christians</color> make no use of a liturgical calendar.
Symbols
Most Christian denominations have not generally practiced aniconism, the avoidance or prohibition of devotional
images, even if early Jewish Christians, invoking the <color=#3366CC>Decalogue's</color> prohibition of <color=#3366CC>idolatry</color>, avoided figures in their
symbols.
The <color=#3366CC>cross</color>, today one of the most widely recognized symbols, was used by Christians from the earliest times. Tertullian,
in his book De Corona, tells how it was already a tradition for Christians to trace the sign of the cross on their
foreheads. Although the cross was known to the early Christians, the <color=#3366CC>crucifix</color> did not appear in use until the 5th century.
Among the earliest Christian symbols, that of the fish or <color=#3366CC>Ichthys</color> seems to have ranked first in importance, as seen on
monumental sources such as tombs from the first decades of the 2nd century. Its popularity seemingly arose from the
Greek word ichthys (fish) forming an acrostic for the Greek phrase Iesous Christos Theou Yios Soter, (Jesus Christ,
Son of God, Savior), a concise summary of Christian faith.
Other major Christian symbols include the <color=#3366CC>chi-rho monogram</color>, the dove and olive branch (symbolic of the Holy Spirit),
the sacrificial lamb (representing Christ's sacrifice), the <color=#3366CC>vine</color> (symbolizing the connection of the Christian with Christ)
and many others. These all derive from passages of the New Testament.
Baptism
Baptism is the ritual act, with the use of water, by which a person is admitted to membership of the Church. Beliefs on
baptism vary among denominations. Differences occur firstly on whether the act has any spiritual significance. Some,
such as the Catholic and <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox churches</color>, as well as Lutherans and Anglicans, hold to the doctrine of
baptismal regeneration, which affirms that baptism creates or strengthens a person's faith, and is intimately linked to
salvation. <color=#3366CC>Baptists</color> and Plymouth Brethren view baptism as a purely symbolic act, an external public declaration of the
inward change which has taken place in the person, but not as spiritually efficacious. Secondly, there are differences of
opinion on the methodology (or mode) of the act. These modes are: by immersion; if immersion is total, by submersion;
by affusion (pouring); and by aspersion (sprinkling). Those who hold the first view may also adhere to the tradition of
infant baptism; the Orthodox Churches all practice infant baptism and always baptize by total immersion repeated three
times in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Lutheran Church and the Catholic Church also
practice infant baptism, usually by affusion, and using the Trinitarian formula. <color=#3366CC>Anabaptist Christians</color> practice believer's
baptism, in which an adult chooses to receive the ordinance after making a decision to follow Jesus. Anabaptist
denominations such as the <color=#3366CC>Mennonites</color>, <color=#3366CC>Amish</color> and <color=#3366CC>Hutterites</color> use pouring as the mode to administer believer's
baptism, whereas Anabaptists of the <color=#3366CC>Schwarzenau Brethren</color> and River Brethren traditions baptize by immersion.
Prayer
"... 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Lead us not into temptation, but
deliver us from evil'".
In the <color=#3366CC>Gospel of Saint Matthew</color>, Jesus taught the <color=#3366CC>Lord's Prayer</color>, which has been seen as a model for Christian prayer.
The injunction for Christians to pray the Lord's prayer thrice daily was given in the Didache and came to be recited by
Christians at 9 am, 12 pm, and 3 pm.
In the second century Apostolic Tradition, Hippolytus instructed Christians to pray at seven fixed prayer times: "on
rising, at the lighting of the evening lamp, at bedtime, at midnight" and "the third, sixth and ninth hours of the day, being
hours associated with Christ's Passion". Prayer positions, including kneeling, standing, and prostrations have been
used for these seven fixed prayer times since the days of the early Church. Breviaries such as the Shehimo and
Agpeya are used by <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox Christians</color> to pray these canonical hours while facing in the eastward direction
of prayer.
The Apostolic Tradition directed that the sign of the cross be used by Christians during the minor exorcism of <color=#3366CC>baptism</color>,
during ablutions before praying at fixed prayer times, and in times of temptation.
Intercessory prayer is prayer offered for the benefit of other people. There are many intercessory prayers recorded in
the Bible, including prayers of the <color=#3366CC>Apostle Peter</color> on behalf of sick persons and by <color=#3366CC>prophets</color> of the Old Testament in
favor of other people. In the <color=#3366CC>Epistle of James</color>, no distinction is made between the intercessory prayer offered by
ordinary believers and the prominent Old Testament prophet <color=#3366CC>Elijah</color>. The effectiveness of prayer in Christianity derives
from the power of God rather than the status of the one praying.
The ancient church, in both <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> and Western Christianity, developed a tradition of asking for the intercession of
(deceased) saints, and this remains the practice of most <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox</color>, <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color>, and some
<color=#3366CC>Lutheran</color> and <color=#3366CC>Anglican</color> churches. Apart from certain sectors within the latter two denominations, other Churches of the
Protestant Reformation, however, rejected prayer to the saints, largely on the basis of the sole mediatorship of Christ.
The reformer <color=#3366CC>Huldrych Zwingli</color> admitted that he had offered prayers to the saints until his reading of the Bible convinced
him that this was idolatrous.
According to the Catechism of the Catholic Church: "Prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God or the
requesting of good things from God". The <color=#3366CC>Book of Common Prayer</color> in the Anglican tradition is a guide which provides a
set order for services, containing set prayers, scripture readings, and hymns or sung Psalms. Frequently in Western
Christianity, when praying, the hands are placed palms together and forward as in the feudal commendation ceremony.
At other times the older orans posture may be used, with palms up and elbows in.
Marriage
Most Christian churches in the world only support <color=#3366CC>marriage</color> between a man and a woman.
Some Christian churches allow local churches to decide about blessings of same-sex marriage.
Some international networks of Affirming churches support blessings of same-sex marriage, such the Association of
Welcoming and Affirming Baptists, Ecumenical Catholic Church, Metropolitan Community Church, Reconciling
Ministries Network (<color=#3366CC>Methodist</color>), The Covenant Network (<color=#3366CC>Pentecostal</color>).
Scriptures
Christianity, like other religions, has adherents whose beliefs and biblical interpretations vary. Christianity regards the
<color=#3366CC>biblical canon</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Old Testament</color> and the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color>, as the inspired word of God. The traditional view of
inspiration is that God worked through human authors so that what they produced was what God wished to
communicate. The Greek word referring to inspiration in 2Timothy 3:16 is theopneustos, which literally means
"God-breathed".
Some believe that divine inspiration makes present Bibles inerrant, while others claim inerrancy for the Bible in its
original manuscripts, although none of those are extant. Another closely related view is biblical infallibility or limited
inerrancy, which affirms that the Bible is free of error as a guide to salvation, but may include errors on matters such as
history, geography, or science.
The canon of the Old Testament accepted by Protestant churches, which is only the <color=#3366CC>Tanakh</color> (the canon of the <color=#3366CC>Hebrew</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bible</color>), is shorter than that accepted by the Orthodox and Catholic churches which also include the <color=#3366CC>deuterocanonical</color>
<color=#3366CC>books</color> which appear in the <color=#3366CC>Septuagint</color>, the Orthodox canon being slightly larger than the Catholic; Protestants regard
the latter as <color=#3366CC>apocryphal</color>, important historical documents which help to inform the understanding of words, grammar, and
syntax used in the historical period of their conception. Some versions of the Bible include a separate Apocrypha
section between the Old Testament and the New Testament. The New Testament, originally written in <color=#3366CC>Koine Greek</color>,
contains 27 books which are agreed upon by all major churches.
Some denominations have additional canonical holy scriptures beyond the Bible, including the standard works of the
Latter Day Saints movement and <color=#3366CC>Divine Principle</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Unification Church</color>.
Catholic interpretation
In antiquity, two schools of exegesis developed in Alexandria and Antioch. The Alexandrian interpretation, exemplified
by <color=#3366CC>Origen</color>, tended to read Scripture <color=#3366CC>allegorically</color>, while the Antiochene interpretation adhered to the literal sense,
holding that other meanings (called <color=#3366CC>theoria</color>) could only be accepted if based on the literal meaning.
Catholic theology distinguishes two senses of scripture: the literal and the spiritual.
The literal sense of understanding scripture is the meaning conveyed by the words of Scripture. The spiritual sense is
further subdivided into:
• The allegorical sense, which includes typology. An example would be the parting of the Red Sea being understood
as a "type" (sign) of baptism.
• The moral sense, which understands the scripture to contain some ethical teaching.
• The anagogical sense, which applies to <color=#3366CC>eschatology</color>, eternity and the <color=#3366CC>consummation of the world</color>.
Regarding <color=#3366CC>exegesis</color>, following the rules of sound interpretation, Catholic theology holds:
• The injunction that all other senses of sacred scripture are based on the literal
• That the historicity of the Gospels must be absolutely and constantly held
• That scripture must be read within the "living Tradition of the whole Church" and
• That "the task of interpretation has been entrusted to the bishops in communion with the successor of Peter, the
<color=#3366CC>Bishop</color> of Rome".
Protestant interpretation
Qualities of Scripture
Many Protestant Christians, such as Lutherans and the Reformed, believe in the doctrine of sola scriptura—that the
Bible is a self-sufficient revelation, the final authority on all Christian doctrine, and <color=#3366CC>revealed all truth</color> necessary for
salvation; other Protestant Christians, such as Methodists and Anglicans, affirm the doctrine of prima scriptura which
teaches that Scripture is the primary source for Christian doctrine, but that "tradition, experience, and reason" can
nurture the Christian religion as long as they are in harmony with the Bible. Protestants characteristically believe that
ordinary believers may reach an adequate understanding of Scripture because Scripture itself is clear in its meaning (or
"perspicuous"). Martin Luther believed that without God's help, Scripture would be "enveloped in darkness". He
advocated for "one definite and simple understanding of Scripture". <color=#3366CC>John Calvin</color> wrote, "all who refuse not to follow the
Holy Spirit as their guide, find in the Scripture a clear light". Related to this is "efficacy", that Scripture is able to lead
people to faith; and "sufficiency", that the Scriptures contain everything that one needs to know to obtain salvation and
to live a Christian life.
Original intended meaning of Scripture
Protestants stress the meaning conveyed by the words of Scripture, the historical-grammatical method. The
historical-grammatical method or grammatico-historical method is an effort in <color=#3366CC>Biblical hermeneutics</color> to find the intended
original meaning in the text. This original intended meaning of the text is drawn out through examination of the passage
in light of the grammatical and syntactical aspects, the historical background, the literary genre, as well as theological
(canonical) considerations. The historical-grammatical method distinguishes between the one original meaning and the
significance of the text. The significance of the text includes the ensuing use of the text or application. The original
passage is seen as having only a single meaning or sense. As Milton S. Terry said: "A fundamental principle in
grammatico-historical exposition is that the words and sentences can have but one significance in one and the same
connection. The moment we neglect this principle we drift out upon a sea of uncertainty and conjecture". Technically
speaking, the grammatical-historical method of interpretation is distinct from the determination of the passage's
significance in light of that interpretation. Taken together, both define the term (Biblical) hermeneutics. Some Protestant
interpreters make use of typology.
Demographics
With around 2.3 billion adherents according to a 2020 estimation by Pew Research Center, split into three main
branches of Catholic, Protestant, and Eastern Orthodox, Christianity is the world's largest religion. High birth rates and
conversions in the <color=#3366CC>global South</color> were cited as the reasons for the Christian population growth. For the last hundred
years, the Christian share has stood at around 33% of the world population. This masks a major shift in the
demographics of Christianity; large increases in the developing world have been accompanied by substantial declines
in the developed world, mainly in Western Europe and North America. Based on the 2020 population estimate,
Christians comprise 28.8% of the <color=#3366CC>world's population</color>. 46.8% of the Christian population is concentrated in 10 countries:

<color=#3366CC>United States</color> (over 210 million), <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color> (over 160 million), <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color> (over 110 million), <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color> and <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> (each one

over 100 million), <color=#3366CC>Nigeria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Congo</color> (each one over 90 million), <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color> (over 70 million), <color=#3366CC>South Africa</color> (over 50
million) and <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> (over 40 million).
Based on a 2015 Pew Research Center study, within the next four decades, Christianity will remain the largest religion;
and by 2050, the Christian population is expected to exceed 3 billion. According to some scholars, Christianity ranks at
first place in net gains through <color=#3366CC>religious conversion</color>. As a percentage of Christians, the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color> and <color=#3366CC>Orthodoxy</color>
(both <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> and <color=#3366CC>Oriental</color>) are declining in some parts of the world (though Catholicism is growing in Asia, in Africa,
vibrant in Eastern Europe, etc.), while <color=#3366CC>Protestants</color> and other Christians are on the rise in the developing world. The
so-called popular Protestantism is one of the fastest growing religious categories in the world. Nevertheless,
Catholicism will also continue to grow to 1.63 billion by 2050, according to Todd Johnson of the Center for the Study of
Global Christianity. Africa alone, by 2015, will be home to 230 million African Catholics. According to Pew Research
Center, Africa is expected to be home to 1.1 billion African Christians by 2050.
In 2010, 87% of the world's Christian population lived in countries where Christians are in the majority, while 13% of the
world's Christian population lived in countries where Christians are in the minority. Christianity is the predominant
religion in Europe, the Americas, Oceania, and Sub-Saharan Africa. There are also large Christian communities in

other parts of the world, such as <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Middle East and North Africa</color>, <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>. In Asia, it is the dominant religion in Armenia, Cyprus, Georgia, East Timor, and the Philippines.
However, it is declining in some areas including the northern and western United States, some areas in Oceania
(Australia and New Zealand), northern Europe (including Great Britain, Scandinavia and other places), France,
Germany, Canada, and some parts of Asia (especially the Middle East, due to the Christian emigration, and Macau).
The total Christian population is not decreasing in <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color> and the <color=#3366CC>southern United States</color>, however, the percentage of
the population identifying as Christian is in decline. Since the fall of communism, the proportion of Christians has been
largely stable in <color=#3366CC>Central Europe</color>, except in the <color=#3366CC>Czech Republic</color>. On the other hand, Christianity is growing rapidly in
both numbers and percentages in Eastern Europe, China, other Asian countries, <color=#3366CC>Sub-Saharan Africa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color>,

<color=#3366CC>North Africa</color> (<color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color>), <color=#3366CC>Gulf Cooperation Council</color> countries, <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>.
Despite a decline in adherence in the <color=#3366CC>West</color>, Christianity remains the dominant religion in the region, with about 70% of
that population identifying as Christian. Christianity remains the largest religion in <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color>, where 71% of
Western Europeans identified themselves as Christian in 2018. A 2011 Pew Research Center survey found that 76% of
Europeans, 73% in Oceania and about 86% in the Americas (90% in Latin America and 77% in North America)
identified themselves as Christians. By 2020, 120 countries and territories in the world had Christian majorities.
There are many charismatic movements that have become well established over large parts of the world, especially
Africa, Latin America, and Asia. Since 1900, primarily due to conversion, Protestantism has spread rapidly in Africa,
Asia, Oceania, and Latin America. From 1960 to 2000, the global growth of the number of reported <color=#3366CC>Evangelical</color>
<color=#3366CC>Protestants</color> grew three times the world's population rate, and twice that of <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>. According to the historian <color=#3366CC>Geoffrey</color>
<color=#3366CC>Blainey</color> from the <color=#3366CC>University of Melbourne</color>, since the 1960s there has been a substantial increase in the number of
conversions from Islam to Christianity, mostly to the <color=#3366CC>Evangelical</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pentecostal</color> forms. Significant numbers of Muslim
converts to Christianity can be found in Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Central Asia (including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and
other countries), Indonesia, Malaysia, the Middle East (including Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and other countries), North
Africa (including Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia), Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Western World (including Albania,
Belgium, France, Germany, Kosovo, the Netherlands, Russia, Scandinavia, United Kingdom, the United States, and
other western countries). It is also reported that Christianity is popular among people of different backgrounds in Africa
and Asia; according to a report by the Singapore Management University, more people in Southeast Asia are
converting to Christianity, many of them young and having a <color=#3366CC>university degree</color>. According to scholar Juliette Koning
and Heidi Dahles of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam there is a "rapid expansion" of Christianity in Singapore, China, Hong
Kong, Taiwan, Indonesia, Malaysia, and South Korea. According to scholar Terence Chong from the Institute of
Southeast Asian Studies, since the 1980s Christianity is expanding in China, Singapore, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia,
Taiwan, South Korea, and Vietnam.
In most countries in the developed world, church attendance among people who continue to identify themselves as
Christians has been falling over the last few decades. Some sources view this as part of a drift away from traditional
membership institutions, while others link it to signs of a decline in belief in the importance of religion in general.
Europe's Christian population, though in decline, still constitutes the largest geographical component of the religion.
According to data from the 2012 European Social Survey, around a third of European Christians say they attend
services once a month or more. Conversely, according to the World Values Survey, about more than two-thirds of Latin
American Christians, and about 90% of African Christians (in Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa and Zimbabwe)
said they attended church regularly. According to a 2018 study by the Pew Research Center, Christians in Africa and
